title: 42 state AGs are trying to stop Character.AI from selling users’ chats
author: Terrence O’Brien
contentSnippet: A coalition of 42 state attorneys general is trying to prevent Character.AI from selling off user data as it navigates Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings. In a deluge of nearly identical press releases, the various AGs accuse the company of planning to auction off “the private chat histories of more than 21 million U.S. accounts — more than 2.1 million of them registered to minors — with no safeguards for the people whose conversations are being sold.” In October, Character.AI filed for bankruptcy following years of scandals and legal challenges, including from Disney. Disney ended up buying some of the company’s assets and hiring its CEO, Karandeep Anand, in a sort of “acquihire” arrangement that will also see “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” join the entertainment giant. The Disney deal also faced opposition from a similarly broad coalition of AGs. The main point of contention with Character.AI’s plan to sell its chat data is that it offers no protections for users. The AGs say there are no requirements that the buyer honor existing privacy policies, no avenues for users to delete their data, and no inherent limits on what a buyer could do with that data, including selling it on to yet another party. It doesn’t help that the first bidder has a limited paper trail, having only been established on November 13th, 2026, with no parent company or investors listed. Some states, including New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado, have also passed laws regulating chatbots that Character.AI may be in violation of when they go into effect on January 1st, 2027.

summary.tldr:
A coalition of 42 state attorneys general has intervened in Character.AI’s Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings to block the proposed sale of user data. The AGs allege that the company intends to auction private chat histories from over 21 million U.S. accounts, including 2.1 million accounts belonging to minors, without implementing privacy safeguards or data deletion mechanisms. The coalition argues that the current sale structure lacks requirements for buyers to honor existing privacy policies or restrict the secondary sale of sensitive user information.

This legal challenge follows Character.AI’s October bankruptcy filing, which occurred amid ongoing litigation, including a dispute with Disney. Disney has since executed an 'acquihire' deal to absorb portions of the company’s technical team and hire CEO Karandeep Anand. The AGs have expressed specific concern regarding the primary bidder for the data, which was incorporated on November 13, 2026, and lacks a disclosed parent company or investor base. Furthermore, the sale may conflict with upcoming chatbot regulations in states such as New York, California, Colorado, and Connecticut, which are set to take effect on January 1, 2027.
takeaways: **Affected User Base:** The proposed data sale involves chat histories from 21 million U.S. accounts, with 2.1 million identified as belonging to minors.
**Regulatory Conflict:** The sale faces potential violations of new chatbot privacy laws in New York, Connecticut, California, and Colorado, effective January 1, 2027.
**Acquihire Details:** Disney has acquired select Character.AI assets and hired CEO Karandeep Anand along with a portion of the technical staff.
**Bidder Transparency:** The primary bidder for the user data was established on November 13, 2026, and currently lists no parent company or investors.

title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
author: Simon Willison AI
contentSnippet:
sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite . This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025 . It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics.

Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO . In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck.

sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy!

It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync:

The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most.

Update : Hah! Turns out I wrote about this application of sqlite_rsync back in October 2024 when the tool was first released.

summary.tldr:
sqlite3_rsync is a specialized utility for SQLite designed to facilitate remote database snapshots and synchronization without requiring the local disk space typically needed by the backup API or VACUUM INTO commands. Introduced as an experimental feature in SQLite 3.47.0 (October 2024) and subsequently enhanced in version 3.50.0 (May 2025), the tool enables direct copying of database snapshots over SSH connections to remote machines.

The tool operates on a protocol similar to the standard rsync utility, utilizing cryptographic hashes to identify and transmit only the data that differs between the origin and the replica. The replica sends hashes for pages or groups of pages to the origin; the origin then returns the specific page content that differs or requests finer-grained hashes if a mismatch is detected. While the overhead of exchanging these hashes can cause total network bandwidth to slightly exceed the size of the database—typically by a few percent—it eliminates the requirement for a full local duplicate, making it particularly effective for resource-constrained environments.
takeaways: **Tool Origin:** sqlite3_rsync was first introduced as an experimental feature in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024.
**Version Enhancements:** Significant updates and enhancements to the tool were released in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025.
**Operational Mechanism:** The tool uses a hash-based synchronization protocol over SSH, allowing for incremental updates rather than full file transfers.
**Resource Efficiency:** It bypasses the need for local disk space equivalent to the database size, which is a mandatory requirement for the standard backup API or VACUUM INTO methods.

title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

What Parse 3.5 produces

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training :

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Figure 2. Parse recovers 1

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has released expansions for its compact document understanding model, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, introducing open synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 inference speculator. Parse 3.5 extracts content, reading order, bounding boxes, and structured records for tables and charts—including inferring unlabelled data points from chart geometry—powered by synthetic data generation and a dual-phase training methodology combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).

The training pipeline begins with SFT across text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents, followed by reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with verifiable rewards to improve extraction accuracy, consistency, and completion. In matched development evaluations, RLVR reduced loop-flagged outputs by approximately 77% (from 126 to 29 pages), reduced outputs hitting the 9,000-token limit from 185 to 35, and improved the overall score from 66.24 to 71.38. Technical optimizations include NaViT image input preprocessing, a visual adapter replacing encoder-decoder cross-attention, grouped-query attention with 8 key/value heads (GQA-8), a multi-token prediction (MTP) head, and the DFlash2 speculator.

Running on a single H200 in BF16, DFlash2 utilizes a draft model proposing up to 32 tokens ahead, averaging about 14 accepted draft tokens per verification step. This increases native single-pass throughput to 20.44 pages/s at concurrency 512 (compared to 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 2.98 pages/s for Parse 2.0). NVIDIA also open-sourced three training datasets: Synthetic Charts V1 (9.98M examples), Synthetic Tables V1 (1M examples), and OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 (7.9M examples), alongside fine-tuning recipes incorporating NeMo Automodel SFT, NeMo RL GRPO, and vLLM.
takeaways: **Open Dataset Releases:** NVIDIA open-sourced Synthetic Charts V1 (9.98M examples), Synthetic Tables V1 (1M examples), and OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 (7.9M examples) containing images, annotations, and training formats.

**RLVR Performance Gains:** Reinforcement learning via GRPO reduced looping outputs by 77% (126 down to 29 pages), decreased max-token truncations from 185 to 35, and raised overall benchmark score from 66.24 to 71.38.

**Inference & Speculator Speeds:** Using a single H200 in BF16 at concurrency 512, DFlash2 speculative decoding increases throughput to 20.44 pages/s (6.86x Parse 2.0 speed), proposing up to 32 tokens ahead with ~14 accepted draft tokens on average.

**Architectural Optimizations:** Parse 3.5 utilizes NaViT preprocessing, a visual adapter replacing encoder-decoder cross-attention, GQA-8 attention-cache memory reduction, and a multi-token prediction (MTP) head.
**Multi-Pass Processing Modes:** Optional double-pass and triple-pass workflows crop and re-parse dense tables or complex charts, adding 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single-pass execution.

title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
author: Mingzhe Du, Thong Thanh Nguyen, Nguyen Tran Cong Duy, See-Kiong Ng, Luu Anh Tuan
contentSnippet:
Authors: Mingzhe Du , Thong Thanh Nguyen , Nguyen Tran Cong Duy , See-Kiong Ng , Luu Anh Tuan

Abstract: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Mingzhe Du, Thong Thanh Nguyen, Nguyen Tran Cong Duy, See-Kiong Ng, and Luu Anh Tuan published a paper titled "Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models," evaluating 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models across 17 tasks and 14 languages. Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return option probabilities for typed queries, utilized directly by routers and guardrails via probability thresholding.

The evaluation reveals that every model experiences accuracy drops in non-English languages—ranging from approximately 2 points for high-resource languages up to 8 points in Tamil—while model confidence declines by only half as much. Consequently, a threshold calibrated for 95% accuracy in English results in actual accuracy dropping to 90% in Tamil. Performance degradation is determined by the specific language and base model rather than overall leaderboard rankings. Across 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skills learned in English successfully transferred to other languages, and a few thousand target-language items reduced large losses; however, neither expanded training data nor full-parameter tuning entirely closed the performance gap.

Additionally, the study found that test items answered via LLM-based translations rather than human translations consistently achieved higher accuracy across all 23 benchmark-language pairs compared, demonstrating that LLM-translated test sets systematically understate the true cross-lingual performance gap.
takeaways: **Evaluated Models & Scope:** Tested 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models across 17 distinct tasks spanning 14 different languages.

**Accuracy vs. Confidence Drop:** Accuracy decreases by roughly 2 points in high-resource languages and up to 8 points in Tamil, while confidence falls by only half that margin, causing a 95% English-calibrated threshold to yield 90% accuracy in Tamil.

**Fine-Tuning Limits:** 81 controlled fine-tuning runs showed that task skills transfer from English and a few thousand target-language items narrow losses, but neither massive data scaling nor full-parameter tuning eliminates the cross-lingual gap.

**Translation Artifacts:** Test items translated by LLMs rather than humans consistently show higher accuracy across all 23 evaluated benchmark-language pairs, indicating LLM-translated test sets understate multilingual performance deficits.

title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
author: Xipeng Qiu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Xipeng Qiu

Abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.

Notes: Author-revised preprint; journal version published in AI Plus; 20 pages, 3 figures, and 3 tables; position paper and narrative survey

summary.tldr:
In a new position paper published in AI Plus, Xipeng Qiu formalizes 'context scaling' as a critical third pillar of AI development, distinct from traditional pretraining (Bθ) and decision-time scaling (Bd). The author argues that current AI failures often stem from a mismatch between necessary task state and the context actually available to the model at inference. By defining the model-infrastructure pair as the primary unit of analysis, the paper introduces a framework governed by three budgets: training, decision-time, and context-infrastructure (Bc), with the latter focusing on the capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, and persist deployment state.

The framework categorizes context failures into four types—availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization—and maps them across a five-operation context lifecycle. Qiu proposes that researchers evaluate systems using utility-cost curves and controlled budget interventions rather than focusing solely on model parameters. The paper advocates for a research agenda centered on grounded reporting, the collection of interaction-data, and the development of full-cost infrastructure models to support persistent, adaptive systems.
takeaways: **Framework Definition:** AI systems are modeled as Pθ(d|c), where performance is constrained by three distinct budgets: training (Bθ), decision-time (Bd), and context-infrastructure (Bc).
**Failure Taxonomy:** Context-related AI failures are classified into four specific categories: availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization.
**Unit of Analysis:** The paper shifts the focus from isolated model weights to the 'model-infrastructure pair' as the fundamental unit for evaluating system performance.
**Evaluation Methodology:** The author proposes using utility-cost curves and controlled budget interventions to measure the effectiveness of context-scaling efforts.

title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
author: Rangarajan Ramesh, Yongchao Huang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component and finds that the largest gains come from combining hard checks with candidate comparison: on tasks where the first sampled answer is often broken or unsafe, this pairing lifts joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 (retrieval-augmented QA) and code-generation safety by up to +0.28 (CWEval), with the size of the gain tracking how weak the first sample is, falling to near zero or slightly negative where it is already strong. The per-task layer that selects and weights the softer checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives. This builds a unified scoring framework, together with an ablation that identifies the grounded hard checks, not the soft-factor configuration, as the source of the gain.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced a constraint-aware test-time scoring framework (arXiv:2611.33161v1) designed to select the best candidate answers from Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by combining hard checks with soft-factor scoring. The framework architecture comprises three distinct components: a drafting model that generates candidate outputs, a configuring model that selects and weights task-specific checks, and scoring models that evaluate properties uncomputable by standard grounded tools.

The authors evaluated the framework across four diverse domains: secure and correct code generation using CWEval, robot manipulation planning using safety-augmented LIBERO variants, competitive programming through hidden tests on LiveCodeBench, and retrieval-augmented question answering via HotpotQA. An ablation study revealed that the primary performance gains stem specifically from combining hard checks with candidate comparison rather than from the per-task configuration layer, which added no measurable value over simpler alternatives. On tasks with weak initial samples, this combination improved joint correctness and safety metrics by up to +0.21 for retrieval-augmented QA and up to +0.28 for CWEval code-generation safety, with gains scaling inversely with the baseline strength of the initial sample.
takeaways: **Core Architecture:** The adaptive scoring framework consists of a drafting model for candidate generation, a configuring model for task-specific check selection, and scoring models for ungrounded properties.

**Evaluated Benchmarks:** Tested across four tasks: CWEval (secure coding), LIBERO (robot manipulation with safety variants), LiveCodeBench (competitive programming hidden tests), and HotpotQA (document-retrieved QA).
**Performance Gains:** Combining hard checks with candidate comparison lifted joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 on retrieval-augmented QA and up to +0.28 on CWEval code-generation safety.

**Ablation Findings:** The per-task layer that selects and weights softer checks added no measurable value over simpler alternatives, proving that grounded hard checks drive the performance improvements.

title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
author: Charles Arnal, Ahmad Rammal, Niket Patel, Fabian Gloeckle, Bartosz Piotrowski, Amaury Hayat, Julia Kempe, R\'emi Munos, Vivien Cabannes
contentSnippet:
Authors: Charles Arnal , Ahmad Rammal , Niket Patel , Fabian Gloeckle , Bartosz Piotrowski , Amaury Hayat , Julia Kempe , Rémi Munos , Vivien Cabannes

Abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at this https URL

Notes: First authors listed in randomized order

summary.tldr:
Researchers from Google DeepMind and NYU, including Charles Arnal, Julia Kempe, and Rémi Munos, have introduced AutoformBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI systems on end-to-end Lean 4 formalization. Unlike existing benchmarks that focus on isolated theorem proving within the pre-existing Mathlib ecosystem, AutoformBench requires agents to construct the necessary definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure required to connect a result to a formal library. The dataset comprises 341 formalization tasks sourced from 24 advanced mathematical texts, each verified and audited by Lean-experienced mathematicians.

Technically, the benchmark forces models to move beyond simple theorem translation by providing an informal proof while requiring the agent to build the formal environment from scratch. Evaluation of frontier models on AutoformBench reveals that performance is primarily gated by an agent's ability to synthesize missing formal infrastructure rather than the specific mathematical domain of the problem. The authors suggest that this 'shared difficulty frontier' highlights a critical gap in current LLM capabilities regarding the structural requirements of formal mathematical development.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** Contains 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks derived from 24 distinct advanced mathematical sources.
**Methodological Shift:** Evaluates the ability to build supporting definitions and intermediate lemmas rather than just isolated theorem proving.
**Evaluation Protocol:** Agents are provided with informal proofs and must translate them into Lean while constructing the required supporting infrastructure.
**Performance Insight:** Success on the benchmark is primarily determined by an agent's capacity to construct missing formal infrastructure across various mathematical domains.

title: General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning
author: Jingzhi Gong, Jie M. Zhang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have released a study (arXiv:2611.33190v1) evaluating the efficacy of general-purpose decision models, specifically the 'Jev' model, in the context of AI configuration tuning. The study examines whether these models can effectively replace or augment traditional tuning strategies by acting as optimizers, performance predictors, or region guiders across eight distinct AI tuning tasks.

Performance benchmarks indicate that Jev struggles to compete with conventional methods in direct optimization and prediction tasks. Conventional optimizers achieved rank 1 in six of the eight tested scenarios, while established performance predictors outperformed Jev in seven. However, Jev demonstrated utility as a 'region guider,' successfully identifying configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by native tuners. This quality improvement comes at the trade-off of increased decision latency and higher API costs, suggesting that general-purpose models are currently best suited for specific guidance roles rather than end-to-end tuning automation.
takeaways: **Comparative Performance:** Conventional optimizers outperformed Jev in 75% (6 of 8) of the tested tuning tasks.
**Predictor Benchmarks:** Established performance predictors proved superior to Jev in 87.5% (7 of 8) of the evaluated tasks.
**Region Guidance Utility:** Jev provides measurable quality gains in perplexity reduction when used specifically for region guidance, despite higher computational and API costs.

**Strategic Recommendation:** The study advises retaining conventional predictors for standard tuning workflows while reserving general-purpose decision models for targeted guidance where quality gains justify the additional latency and expense.

title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
author: Catarina Botelho, Ant\'onio Farinhas, John Mendon\c{c}a, Areti Vassilopoulos, In\^es Gon\c{c}alves, Maya D'Eon, Hugo Pitorro, Laura Cabello, Carrie Spadine, Nuno M. Guerreiro, Ricardo Rei
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.

We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations.

title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
author: Baptiste Juran, Dimitri Kachler, Damien Sileo
contentSnippet:
Authors: Baptiste Juran , Dimitri Kachler , Damien Sileo

Abstract: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof. A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.

Notes: 24 pages, 5 figures. Code/data: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Baptiste Juran, Dimitri Kachler, and Damien Sileo have identified a critical flaw in procedurally generated logic datasets: the 'planted proof' method often overstates the actual reasoning depth required to solve a problem. By auditing eight existing datasets, including ProofWriter, Blocksworld, FLDx2, and ZebraLogic, the authors demonstrate that many problems labeled with high depth requirements can actually be solved via significantly shorter 'shortcuts' or require only a fraction of the intended inference steps. The study introduces a new verification framework that computes the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs, and indispensable premises for any given problem, exporting verifiable certificates for each.

To address these inconsistencies, the authors developed a construction method that guarantees a requested proof structure by utilizing a catalog of pre-verified shortcuts. This approach ensures that every generated problem is checked in full and accompanied by a certificate. When training Qwen3 models ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, the researchers found that mixing these certified problem types—including model-checking tasks that standard forward generation fails to produce—results in superior transfer performance compared to traditional FLDx2-style derivation data. The findings suggest that data quality and structural integrity are more critical for reasoning performance than simply increasing the stated depth of training samples.
takeaways: **Dataset Audit Findings:** Analysis of FLDx2 revealed problems labeled as depth 5 that often require only two specific rule applications, while ZebraLogic problems frequently contain answers requiring no specific inference steps.
**Verification Framework:** The authors implemented a system to compute the shortest proof, minimal proof counts, and indispensable premises, providing independent certificates for each problem.
**Model Performance:** Training Qwen3 models (0.6B to 8B parameters) on mixtures of certified problem types yielded better transfer performance than training on standard FLDx2-style derivation data.
**Construction Methodology:** The new approach uses a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set to ensure every generated problem adheres to a specific, requested logical structure.

title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
author: Ross Murphy, Gabriel Brostow
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ross Murphy , Gabriel Brostow

Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Ross Murphy and Gabriel Brostow have introduced evidence supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) within 'Jacobian-space' (J-space), suggesting that AI models converge toward a shared internal representation of the world regardless of modality. By analyzing the Jacobian lens—which maps vocabulary words or image classes to vectors in a model's hidden state that maximize output probability—the authors demonstrate that J-spaces across vision and language models are approximately equivalent up to a rotation.

The study reveals that a single rotation matrix, calibrated on a subset of tokens, can map the J-space of one model onto another with high fidelity. This transformation holds for unseen tokens and classes, allowing for cross-modal manipulation. For instance, rotating a vector from a text-only language model into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model successfully alters the model's object identification within specific image regions. Similarly, applying these rotations to image generators modifies generated content, and mapping these vectors into an ImageNet classifier significantly boosts the corresponding class scores, confirming that models share not just static representations, but functional mechanisms for acting upon those representations.
takeaways: **J-space Definition:** The collection of vectors in a transformer's hidden state that maximize the probability of a specific output word or image class.
**Rotation Equivalence:** J-spaces across disparate vision and language models can be aligned using a single rotation matrix fitted on a subset of data.
**Cross-Modal Utility:** Rotated vectors from text-only models can influence visual outputs in vision-language models and image generators, as well as class predictions in pure vision classifiers.
**Functional Convergence:** The findings extend the Platonic Representation Hypothesis by suggesting models converge on how they act on world representations, not just how they store them.

title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
author: Ben Moore
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.

summary.tldr:
A new research study (arXiv:2611.33322v1) audits brand recall and category accuracy for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories using language models without external retrieval. On Gemma 4 12B, category prompts successfully elicit 510 brands, representing 51.0% of the dataset. When evaluated using a five-candidate category probe, the model ranks the correct reference label first for 787 brands, places a distractor first for 194, and shows little separation for 19.

Among the 981 separated rankings, the classification error rate stands at 19.8%, which drops significantly to 3.5% for the 547 brands exhibiting a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin greater than 0.6. Exploratory regressions link technical coverage to recall and an owned-properties composite to category accuracy, though these composites utilize differing adjustment sets and do not prove causality. Across four successive Gemma model generations, measured recall progresses from 39.8% to 44.3%, 51.1%, and finally 51.0%. Additionally, a representation-based sentiment measure demonstrates virtually no linear association with actual customer ratings, yielding a correlation coefficient of r=0.03 across 921 evaluated brands.

The findings demonstrate that language models can name a brand without classifying it correctly, supporting the necessity of reporting recall and category accuracy as distinct metrics. Furthermore, the authors note that failing to elicit a brand does not confirm its absence from the underlying model parameters or training data.

**Gemma 4 12B Performance:** Category prompts without external retrieval elicit 510 brands (51.0%), while a five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands.
**Classification Error Rates:** The error rate across 981 separated rankings is 19.8%, falling to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin exceeding 0.6.
**Gemma Generation Progression:** Measured recall across four generations of Gemma models is recorded at 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1%, and 51.0%.
**Sentiment Correlation:** A representation-based sentiment measure shows minimal linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921).

title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
author: Luiz G. A. Alves, Aaron Vermeersch
contentSnippet:
Authors: Luiz G. A. Alves , Aaron Vermeersch

Abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Luiz G. A. Alves and Aaron Vermeersch have introduced a supervised learning framework designed to generate reliable confidence scores for LLM-based agents, addressing the issue of overconfident, incorrect model outputs. The approach utilizes a linear confidence score head attached to the final-layer hidden state of a frozen 2B-parameter LLM backbone, or alternatively, text-only metamodels for closed-source systems. By predicting the correctness of generated answers, the system enables automated gating, where high-confidence responses are processed directly and uncertain outputs are routed for human review.

Testing was conducted on a dataset comprised of approximately 98% SQuAD and 2% TruthfulQA. The researchers found that while prompted confidence scores often appear well-calibrated, they lack the necessary resolution for effective thresholding. The proposed linear confidence score head outperformed all tested baselines and metamodels, successfully automating a larger fraction of the workload while maintaining high accuracy targets. Although the authors noted that transferability to unseen datasets remains modest, the method provides a more robust mechanism for safety and compliance gating than existing alternatives.
takeaways: **Architecture:** A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of a frozen 2B-parameter LLM backbone.
**Dataset Composition:** Evaluation was performed on graded answers consisting of 98% SQuAD and 2% TruthfulQA.
**Performance:** The linear confidence score head outperformed all tested baselines and metamodels in automating workloads at high accuracy targets.
**Limitation:** The framework exhibits modest transferability when applied to unseen datasets.
**Application:** The system is designed to gate LLM-based agent decisions for safety, compliance, and human-in-the-loop routing.

title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
author: Siddharth Arya, Kshitij Jain
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI models vary enormously in capability and price. Model routing exploits this by sending easier tasks to cheaper models. However, a single agentic task often combines easy and difficult subtasks, making one model choice for the entire task inefficient. We introduce partial routing, which guides a frontier lead model to delegate suitable subtasks to a cheaper worker model. From both models' past runs, we identify recurring subtasks and measure each model's quality and cost on them. These measurements produce delegation guidance, with a parameter, $\delta$, controlling how much is delegated. The lead decides when and what to delegate during execution, without training either model. On held-out tasks from ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0, partial routing achieves higher mean task performance than the lead alone and task-level routing. With $\delta = 0.75$, it raises the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost, and its Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. Giving the lead only the subtask breakdown, without a worker, also reduces cost on both benchmarks and raises the Terminal-Bench pass rate. These results show that analysis of past runs can support more efficient planning and more effective delegation, with little cost and implementation overhead.

title: Collaborative Language Models for Semantic IoT Data Processing: Validation through Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition
author: Mohsen Shirali, Kean Ooi, Anna Knab, Mohammadreza Fani Sani, Estefania Serral
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems generate low-level sensor observations that are not directly suitable for process analysis and must first be transformed into semantically meaningful events. This paper investigates collaborative language models as a zero-shot semantic abstraction layer for converting such observations into higher-level event and activity labels. We propose a five-stage workflow comprising semantic mapping, semantic aggregation, temporal and contextual aggregation, specialized reasoning, and final event abstraction. The resulting labels and contextual information can subsequently be represented as event records for downstream Process Mining (PM) tasks. The approach is evaluated through Human Activity Recognition on the CASAS Aruba smart home dataset using eleven workflow configurations. The experiments show that collaboration alone does not guarantee improved performance: general-purpose auxiliary SLMs can degrade recognition, whereas assigning complementary specialist roles leads to better results and allows a smaller final classifier to retain much of the performance of a larger model. The selected workflow achieves a macro F1 of 0.643 in the 1.5-day comparison and 0.567 (weighted F1 0.680) in a one-week evaluation. Although trained ML approaches remain more accurate on this dataset, the results demonstrate a different design point: modular semantic event abstraction using off-the-shelf models without task-specific parameter fine-tuning. The findings indicate that the structure of LM collaboration and task decomposition is more important than simply increasing the number of participating models.

title: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion
author: Jeremy Canale
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an end-to-end empirical study of dynamic reasoning in next-generation detection and response pipelines, evaluating how static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents perform under strict human-analyst attention budgets (Recall at B alerts/day). Across 56 reproducible experiments spanning a multi-layer enterprise-and-cloud simulator and four public datasets (SOREL-20M, BODMAS, LANL, and DARPA Transparent Computing), we test twelve architectural claims governing modern fleet-scale defense. First, we show that fleet growth halves recall at a fixed analyst budget even at negligible compute cost (<$0.0003 per million events), and that rarity-weighted graph risk propagation outperforms GraphSAGE without neural training. Second, evaluating frontier reasoning models (Gemini) and fine-tuned open-weight models (Qwen3-4B) for alert triage reveals that unconstrained LLM auto-closure eliminates 90% of false positives while silently discarding 31-44% of true attack cases. Third, post-training with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) causes severe reward hacking on unseen attack classes, suppressing up to 86% of novel attacks compared to two-epoch supervised fine-tuning. Finally, against an adaptive adversary generating plausible cover stories in benign telemetry fields, LLM triage evasion rises sharply unless gated by a deterministic policy harness prior to model invocation.

title: CA-RAG: Constraint-Aligned Retrieval for Structurally Faithful Long-Form Generation
author: Vimal Kumar Kumar, Meghana Kshirsagar, Conor Ryan
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically optimises evidence selection for semantic relevance, whereas compliance-sensitive long-form generation also requires evidence supporting explicit structural obligations. Semantically relevant retrieval may therefore omit information needed for mandatory downstream clauses. We propose Constraint-Aligned RAG (CA-RAG), a retrieval-conditioning framework that augments section-specific queries with ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations before evidence selection. Retrieval-only evaluation with manually annotated evidence shows consistent improvements across retrieval budgets. At $k=6$, CA-RAG increases Precision@$k$ from $0.5268$ to $0.5692$, pooled Recall@$k$ from $0.5402$ to $0.5950$, and F1@$k$ from $0.5389$ to $0.5672$ over standard RAG. Generation experiments further show improvements in compliance and reliability in several model--domain settings, while generation-only constraints achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results indicate that structurally aligned retrieval can improve evidence sufficiency in compliance-sensitive long-form generation.

title: Learning to Reason in Real-Time
author: Xavier Schneider, Benjamin Schneider, Sun Sun, Olga Vechtomova, Victor Zhong
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they currently do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines. Across time pressures, we outperform the strongest non-RRT baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution and 55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks in two real-time environments: Frogger and Snake. These results demonstrate that we can teach agents to balance reasoning and responsiveness under real-time constraints, and that RRT opens a broad, new set of capabilities for real-time agents.

title: PeerReveal: Learning to Generalize in AI Peer Review Detection
author: Zi Li, Andr\'e V. Duarte, Lei Li
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can we distinguish fully AI-generated reviews from those using AI only to rewrite human judgement? Furthermore, can we do so reliably when reviews are generated from diverse AI models and workflows across scientific domains? To this end, we introduce PeerReveal, a new detector that grounds its decisions in learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims drawn from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, complemented by review-level textual signals. We evaluate PeerReveal on PeerShift, a new, challenging test set of 5,430 reviews spanning multiple domains, including machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, combining variation in disciplinary review conventions with diverse AI review-production mechanisms. With regular training, PeerReveal achieves 70.52% pooled Macro-F1 on this benchmark, improving over the strongest baseline by 11.48 points. We develop an effective and practical adversarial training framework that further improves the detector's generalization using a small local generator optimized to produce challenging reviews, raising pooled Macro-F1 from 70.52% to 82.40%. These results show that robust AI-review detection benefits from richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more challenging generation processes.

title: FIG-MAC: A Fine-grained Inspiration Graph Empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation
author: Siyuan Chen, Yuping Gao, Tai Huang, Yuling Zhou, Dongyu Su, Tongguan Wang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated Scientific Hypothesis Generation (ASHG) leveraging large language models (LLMs) aims to harness their strengths in knowledge integration, logical reasoning, and text generation for efficiently producing innovative, verifiable scientific hypotheses. However, existing approaches face three critical limitations: (i) insufficient fine-grained knowledge representation, as unstructured context impairs LLM comprehension and reasoning; (ii) lack of knowledge evolution traceability, constraining the generation of innovative cross-domain conjectures; (iii) absence of human-inspired and role-specialized multi-agent collaboration, failing to leverage the efficient innovation mechanisms arising from cognitive diversity and division of labor among expert roles to complete the full ASHG-evaluation loop. To address these limitations, we propose the Fine-grained Inspiration Graph-empowered Multi-Agent Collaboration framework (FIG-MAC) including: (i) Fine-grained Inspiration Graph module (FIG), to obtain fine-grained structured knowledge representations, where nodes represent academic semantic units and edges encode heuristic relationships among them; (ii) ontology-guided hybrid reasoning module, which follows the FIG ontology to construct structured reasoning paths and uses vector search to enrich them with semantic evidence, to obtain the traceable scientific conjecture paths; (iii) role-specialized Multi-Agent framework, inspired by real scientific teamwork, enabling a closed-loop process of scientific conjecture generation, screening, and validation. Experimental results demonstrate that FIG-MAC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on source diversity, provenance-adjusted novelty, and raw novelty.

title: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements
author: Jiechen Li, Hannah Groos, Brinnae Bent
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33594v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions. By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.

Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons.

Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions.
By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.

title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
author: Yechan Cho, Hyeonsu Lee, Emma Deneuville, Jaeson Jang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically na\"ive animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

title: Controllable CAD Generation and Interactive Editing of Fluid Rotors
author: Shen Chen, Lei Li, Jiajun Sun, Zitian Wang, Huaping Zhang, Peng Wu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-aided design (CAD) provides the geometric foundation for rotors in fluid rotating machinery. However, creating models for different rotors requires different modeling processes, making it difficult to control geometry through design intent and reuse existing models. We introduce VaneCraft, an agent-driven framework for rotor generation, inverse recovery, and editing through a unified analytical representation. The agent interprets design requests and invokes geometric modeling operations. The representation defines geometric controls through meridional geometry and independent boundary angle laws. An anisotropic partial differential equation (PDE) maps these controls to the blade surfaces. Geometric parameter correction (GPC) uses a joint geometric encoder and a parameter decoder to refine controls initialized from rotor category and dimensions. Inverse recovery maps existing CAD to the same geometric controls for reconstruction and continued editing. Experiments demonstrate that VaneCraft supports anisotropy control and parameter editing and outperforms representative baselines in rotor CAD generation tasks. Project page is available on \href{https://github.com/shenchen333/vanecraft}{GitHub}.

title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
author: Zax Shen, Hanling Zhang, Zixu Wang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.

title: The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
author: Adama Njie, Leandro Laperne, Laksh Agarwal, Ali Torkayesh, Sandra Venghaus
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.

title: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory
author: Junhong Huang, Xin Tong, Jun Xia
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many systems index by invoking generative LLMs to rewrite history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs--a step that is (a) costly (thousands of generative calls per build), (b) non-deterministic (undermining reproducibility and giving inconsistent answers across runs), and (c) provenance-erasing (the reader sees synthesized text, not the original turn). We propose MGMem, a framework with no generative indexing calls that replaces this step with a deterministic discriminative-parser pipeline: recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph, question mentions are resolved by a subject-conditioned three-stage resolver, and raw dialogue episodes are returned to the reader. On English multi-session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched-protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls; on the full LongMemEval-S, it remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single-session types among local retrieval comparisons. Code: https://github.com/junhong-h/MGMem

title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
author: Michael Hemenway, Edward W. Wolfe
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.

title: Psychophysics of Duration Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
author: Auss Abbood, Zihao Fu, Nigel Collier
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Studies of time perception in language models focus mainly on text-based settings. Yet multimodal models are increasingly used for tasks that require perceiving the passage of time, making the limits of their temporal perception important to understand. We measure the limits of duration perception from audio against a human baseline to address this gap. Drawing from psychophysics, we operationalise duration perception as a melody recognition task, testing when a melody becomes unrecognisable as it is slowed down. Of 21 tested models, most cannot recognise well-known melodies without labelled in-context examples. With in-context examples, seven recognise melodies reliably, most peaking within the median human recognition band. Generalisation is limited: (i) recognition peaks shift with in-context example speed, (ii) melody titles induce prediction bias, and (iii) providing examples with scientific pitch notation does not prevent accuracy declining at long note durations for most models. In humans, the recognition window is a property of the perceiver; in current models, it is largely a property of the prompt.

title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models
author: Yiming Zhang, Koji Tsuda
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
author: Arushi Gupta, Sheng Liu, James Zou
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.

title: Focus On Facts: Stylistically Invariant and Factually Sensitive Text Embeddings
author: Maximus Adeola
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text embedding models can conflate surface-form similarity with factual identity. Given an altered near-copy with one corrupted fact and a differently worded fact-preserving rewrite, the base model prefers the altered near-copy. We test whether hard-negative contrastive supervision can reduce this surface-similarity shortcut. We construct FOF-Bench, an 83,263-triplet benchmark spanning five domains. Each anchor is paired with an LLM-generated, fact-preserving stylistic rewrite and a matched fact-altered near-copy. We fine-tune FOF-80M (Focus On Facts), an 80M-parameter embedding model, with a triplet contrastive objective that ranks the rewrite above the factual alteration. On 8,327 held-out test triplets, the base model chooses the factually altered text in 99.58% of cases (0.42% factual preference rate; mean separation -0.1650). After fine-tuning, mean positive--negative separation is +0.0329, 98.5% of individual margins move in the intended direction, and the preference rate reaches 29.37%. On DiSC, an external style-transfer corpus, mean cross-style similarity increases from 0.7905 to 0.9559. The model also penalizes omission and transfers poorly to directional tasks such as NLI and summarization. We characterize FOF-80M as a soft factual fingerprint for studying factual retention under stylistic variation, not as a general-purpose factuality metric.

title: FrId\'eo: French News Outlet Ideology Scoring via Multi-Source Evidence Fusion and Distancing-Aware Lexical Scoring
author: Amr Sobhy
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.33266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Outlet ideology is a standard explanatory variable in media framing, media effects, and political communication research, but continuous, ecosystem-wide coverage lets it enter as graded exposure rather than a coarse bin. For France, existing references are either broad but non-analytic or analytic but sparse and source-specific, and none we are aware of offers ecosystem-wide coverage on a unified continuous scale. We contribute FrId\'eo: to our knowledge the first ecosystem-wide continuous ideology scores for the French press, a transparent composite score for 30 French news outlets, fusing nine independent families of evidence with empirical-Bayes-style shrinkage toward a structural prior. For the text-based family we introduce symmetric plain/qualified scoring, which separates the plain use of ideologically loaded vocabulary from its qualified (distanced) use on both sides, a distinction bag-of-words methods miss. The resulting scale runs from L'Humanit\'e on the far left to Valeurs actuelles on the far right; the far-right pole is near-indistinguishable and CNews ties Le Figaro. Because the text family reads current articles, it also captures editorial change that static sources miss, such as the Journal du Dimanche's sharp rightward shift after its 2023 ownership change. The ordering is robust to perturbation and to dropping any single family, and agrees with held-out Media Bias Fact Check labels. We release the scores, confidence intervals, and replication code.
