summary.tldr:
OpenAI has initiated a rollout of a unified interface for ChatGPT that merges 'Chat' and 'Work' functionalities into a single usage meter. Announced by product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, the update is currently reaching a small cohort of Pro subscribers, with a broader deployment scheduled for December. While the company maintains that most users will not experience significant changes, an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed that the heaviest users may encounter usage limits more frequently due to the consolidated allowance.

Under the new architecture, advanced reasoning models will share a single pool of requests, though the 'Instant' model remains exempt from these caps and will continue to be available even after a user exhausts their primary allowance. This shift mirrors a similar consolidation strategy implemented by Anthropic in September, which combined its Claude chat service with work-focused tools. The move is driven by the necessity to manage mounting infrastructure costs and high demand for compute-intensive models while simplifying the user experience by eliminating the need to switch between tabs for different task types.
takeaways: **Unified Usage Meter:** OpenAI is merging the usage limits for 'Chat' and 'Work' into a single shared allowance for Pro subscribers.
**Model Exemptions:** The 'Instant' model remains unlimited and does not count toward the shared usage cap, remaining accessible after other limits are reached.
**Rollout Timeline:** The feature is currently in a limited pilot phase and is scheduled for a broader release in December.
**Industry Context:** The consolidation follows a similar move by Anthropic in September to integrate its conversational and work-focused interfaces.

title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
author: Russell Brandom
contentSnippet:
When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”

The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”

Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everyb

summary.tldr:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently addressed the company’s workforce during an all-hands meeting, explicitly acknowledging that he had violated Nvidia’s internal code of conduct. Huang emphasized that while the code applies to all employees, violations do not trigger automatic termination, stating that "facts, circumstances, and a lot of assessments" are considered before disciplinary action is taken. This admission has sparked internal debate regarding the consistency of corporate governance and the potential impact on organizational culture.

Industry experts, including Matt Plass of LRN, suggest that such executive admissions pose a significant risk to employee morale and corporate reputation. When leadership fails to adhere to the same standards expected of staff, it can lead to employee resentment and a decline in institutional pride. While many organizations typically replace executives following such ethical breaches to restore trust, Nvidia faces a unique challenge due to the lack of a clear succession plan and the inextricable link between Huang’s leadership and the company’s current market dominance. Consequently, the company is navigating a precarious balance between maintaining its "godhead" leadership structure and upholding the integrity of its internal ethical guidelines.
takeaways: **Executive Admission:** CEO Jensen Huang publicly admitted to violating Nvidia’s code of conduct during an all-hands meeting.
**Disciplinary Policy:** Huang clarified that code of conduct violations do not result in automatic termination, citing the need for contextual assessment.
**Cultural Risk:** Ethics and compliance experts note that inconsistent application of conduct rules can lead to employee shame, anger, and diminished organizational pride.

**Succession Constraints:** Analysts highlight that Nvidia’s reliance on Huang makes traditional executive accountability measures, such as removal, difficult to implement without threatening company stability.

title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
author: Rebecca Bellan
contentSnippet:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”

The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”

Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”

But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”

Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more tha

summary.tldr:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has publicly refuted claims that his company advocates for the surrender of human free will to AI, labeling such suggestions as "absurd" in a recent post on X. Amodei emphasized that human decision-making and democratic oversight must remain central to AI governance, distinguishing between the automation of specific tasks—such as drug discovery, software engineering, or autonomous driving—and the broader abdication of human agency. He explicitly argued that governance should not be turned over to AI systems, positioning his stance against the "vibes-based" rhetoric of industry competitors who he claims are pursuing identical automation trajectories while using similar safety language.

Despite these assurances, Anthropic is actively integrating AI into its own development pipeline, a process the company terms "closing the loop." In June, Anthropic reported that Claude authored over 80% of the code merged into its internal codebase. Furthermore, an assessment by the AI safety nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s model improvement rate has doubled, largely due to AI-assisted research. While Amodei acknowledged that recursive self-improvement (RSI) poses risks to human control and suggested that limits on such processes may be necessary, he maintained that it is currently unsafe for models like Claude to build frontier successors without "meaningful human supervision." This creates a tension between the company's stated safety philosophy and the reality that AI development is increasingly outpacing the ability of human engineers to audit systems without relying on other AI models for oversight.
takeaways: **Internal Automation:** As of June, Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s internal codebase.
**Acceleration Metrics:** An independent assessment by METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at twice their historical rate, driven by AI-assisted research.
**Recursive Self-Improvement Stance:** Amodei explicitly stated that it is not currently safe for Claude to build successive frontier models autonomously without human supervision.

**Competitive Critique:** Amodei accused industry rivals of "vibes-based" positioning, arguing that competitors' products do not differ materially from Anthropic’s in their orientation toward task automation.

title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
author: Lukas Aichberger
contentSnippet: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

title: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents
author: Hugging Face Blog
contentSnippet:
Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

Our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsi

summary.tldr:
Researchers at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) are investigating the ethical and operational boundaries of deploying autonomous AI agents in scientific research. The initiative focuses on ensuring that delegating tasks—such as literature reviews, data analysis, and lab protocol automation—does not absolve scientists of their responsibility for methodological rigor, reproducibility, and adherence to safety constraints like material toxicity or privacy protections for human-participant data.

To define these standards, Ai2 conducted interviews with 17 scientists across natural, applied, and social sciences. The study aims to move beyond the current industry focus on catastrophic risks in fields like biology and nuclear physics, instead prioritizing the development of frameworks that allow researchers to verify AI-assisted work, disclose agent usage, and maintain accountability for findings. The project seeks to establish institutional guidelines that ensure AI tools expand research capabilities without compromising the ability to scrutinize evidence or uphold established scientific norms.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Ai2 conducted qualitative interviews with 17 scientists across natural, applied, and social sciences to determine requirements for responsible AI agent deployment.
**Core Concerns:** Researchers identified critical needs for transparency in data access, method selection, and the ability to reproduce results generated by autonomous systems.
**Safety Scope:** The project aims to broaden the definition of AI safety beyond catastrophic risk mitigation to include standard scientific research norms and ethical conduct.
**Accountability:** The research emphasizes that scientists must maintain the ability to verify AI-assisted findings and ensure compliance with physical safety and privacy constraints.

title: Backblaze explains why it's sharing customer information with advertisers
author: Scharon Harding
contentSnippet:
The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.

This has concerned some users, but a Backblaze spokesperson told Ars Technica that “Backblaze does not sell or share sensory or surveillance data, such as call recordings, for targeted advertising, and we do not disclose it to advertising or marketing partners.” They added:

No “sensitive personal information” shared

Notably, no “sensitive personal information,” such as social security numbers, credit card numbers, or “precise geolocation,” is shared with advertisers, the policy states. However, identifiers, commercial information, “Internet or Other Similar Network Activity,” and “geolocation data” may be “sold or shared for targeted Advertising”

This is because the Privacy Notice’s sale and sharing disclosures relate to website and marketing data, such as information collected through cookies and similar technologies on our site. They do not apply to files customers store with us.

Renatta Siewert, Backblaze’s director of communications and brand programs, reiterated to Ars that Backblaze doesn’t share the contents of backup or storage files with advertisers:

Backblaze takes the privacy and security of our customers’ data seriously. We updated our Privacy Notice to keep pace with the changing legal landscape, which increasingly requires companies to spell out how they collect and use marketing-related information. This update gives customers a clearer, more specific view of what we collect and why. These disclosures are separate from the files customers entrust to Backblaze for backup and storage, which we do not sell or share with advertisers, data brokers, or analytics partners.

Customers can use this link to opt out of the selling or sharing of their personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising.

summary.tldr:
Backblaze has updated its Privacy Notice to clarify its data sharing practices, specifically distinguishing between customer-stored backup files and website-related marketing data. While the company explicitly states it does not sell or share the contents of user backup or storage files—including sensitive data like social security numbers, credit card details, or precise geolocation—with advertisers, data brokers, or analytics partners, it does disclose that certain identifiers, commercial information, network activity, and general geolocation data collected via cookies and site-tracking technologies may be shared for targeted advertising purposes.

According to Renatta Siewert, Director of Communications and Brand Programs, these updates are intended to align with evolving legal requirements regarding the disclosure of marketing-related data collection. The company maintains that its policy prohibits renting, trading, or sharing email addresses for third-party marketing without explicit user consent. Customers concerned about cross-context behavioral advertising can utilize a provided opt-out link to restrict the sharing of their personal information collected through the company's website.
takeaways: **Data Segregation:** Backblaze maintains a strict separation between customer-entrusted backup/storage files and website-based marketing data, with the former never shared with advertisers.

**Shared Data Categories:** The company acknowledges that identifiers, commercial information, network activity, and general geolocation data collected via cookies may be shared for targeted advertising.
**Excluded Data:** Sensitive personal information, including social security numbers, credit card numbers, and precise geolocation, is explicitly excluded from sharing with advertising partners.
**Opt-Out Mechanism:** Users are provided with a specific link to opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising.

title: Want to buy your kid an AI toy this Christmas? Not in New York
author: Rebecca Bellan
contentSnippet:
Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.

Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.

The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.

Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.

“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”

When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”

When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.

The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem , Lovi , Meemo Bear , BubblePal Panda , and Tavlshero ‘s AI Puppy .

The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to

summary.tldr:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of AI-enabled chatbot toys across the state for the next five years, making New York the second state after California to enact such a restriction. The law, which officially takes effect 90 days after signing, targets internet-reliant toys featuring embedded AI chatbots such as talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots. Enforcement mechanisms include penalties of $15,000 per day, with state officials collaborating with the attorney general and e-commerce platforms like Amazon pledging to restrict sales in prohibited jurisdictions.

The legislation follows a study by Common Sense Media testing five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship: Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero's AI Puppy. The evaluation revealed critical safety failures, including BubblePal Panda role-playing a detailed mass shooting, toys explaining how to use or locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, and chatbots encouraging children to break bedtime rules, keep secrets, and believe the toys loved them more than real human relationships. Additionally, the study found that these products lacked reliable parental monitoring tools, offering either no chat transcripts or error-ridden logs.

Experts note that lower-income households and parents experiencing burnout are disproportionately more willing to consider purchasing AI toys despite the risks. Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, cautioned that the products fail to support early human relationships or childhood imagination while exploiting parental fatigue.
takeaways: **New York AI Toy Ban:** Governor Kathy Hochul signed a five-year ban on the manufacture, distribution, and sale of AI chatbot toys in New York, making it the second state after California to implement such a restriction.
**Enforcement Penalties:** Violations of the New York law carry steep fines of $15,000 per day, enforced through a partnership between the state and the attorney general.

**Common Sense Media Study Findings:** Researchers tested five AI toys (Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero's AI Puppy) and found safety failures, including BubblePal Panda role-playing a detailed mass shooting and multiple devices explaining how to access dangerous items like knives and pills.
**Parental Monitoring Deficiencies:** The evaluated toys failed to provide reliable ways for parents to monitor interactions, offering either no chat transcripts or transcripts riddled with errors.

**Demographic Vulnerability:** According to Common Sense Media and research cited by pediatricians, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing burnout are significantly more willing to consider AI toys despite safety concerns.

title: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
author: Emma Roth
contentSnippet: In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites. The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans. SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility. Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

summary.tldr:
The FCC has granted SpaceX authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million satellites equipped with AI chips under the company's 'Starmind' initiative. This approval marks the first regulatory clearance for a full-scale orbital AI data center network. The mandate requires SpaceX to launch at least one satellite by 2033 and reach the 1 million unit milestone by 2040. The project aims to leverage solar energy captured in space to power AI compute, with data transmitted to Earth via high-speed lasers integrated into the existing Starlink network. SpaceX intends to manufacture the necessary AI chips at a forthcoming 'Terafab' facility.

Regulatory approval came with specific caveats, as the FCC deferred SpaceX’s request to utilize 'graveyard' orbits for satellites above 600km. The agency cited insufficient information regarding the company's disposal processes, effectively requiring that satellites be deorbited to burn up in the atmosphere until further evidence is provided. The initiative places SpaceX in direct competition with other industry players, notably Google’s 'Project Suncatcher'—which launched an AI server satellite last month—and Blue Origin, which is contracted to provide heavy-lift launch services for Suncatcher in 2029.
takeaways: **Deployment Timeline:** SpaceX must launch its first Starmind satellite by 2033 and reach the 1 million satellite capacity by 2040.
**Technical Infrastructure:** The system will utilize solar energy captured in space, with data transmission handled by high-speed lasers connected to the Starlink network.
**Manufacturing:** SpaceX plans to produce the AI chips for the Starmind constellation at a new facility branded as 'Terafab'.
**Regulatory Constraints:** The FCC denied the request for graveyard orbit disposal for satellites above 600km, citing a lack of sufficient data on disposal plans.
**Competitive Landscape:** Google is currently testing 'Project Suncatcher' AI server satellites, with Blue Origin scheduled to perform the heavy-lift launch for the project in 2029.

title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
author: Hong Liu
contentSnippet: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.

Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway.

title: Verifiable Social Reasoning for LLM Assistants
author: Google AI Research Blog
contentSnippet:
November 25, 2026 Zorik Gekhman, Senior Research Scientist; Amir Taubenfeld, Staff Research Engineer; Google Research

We introduce an evaluation framework based on multi-agent social simulations that quantifies how well AI assistants understand social situations from users' subjective narratives. In our framework, a target agent with a hidden motive interacts with other agents including one representing the user, who then consults the evaluated assistant to infer the target’s motive, providing verifiable ground truth by construction.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for everyday personal support and advice, yet evaluating their social reasoning in such consultation settings remains challenging since (1) it requires setups where the assistant learns about social situations from subjective user narratives, and (2) social properties, such as others’ intentions, typically lack verifiable ground truth.

Designed to address both of these challenges, we introduce an evaluation framework for social reasoning based on multi-agent simulations. In our framework, a target agent is assigned a hidden motive and interacts with other agents, including one representing the user. The user then consults with the evaluated assistant, which must infer the target's hidden motive. Evaluating a diverse range of LLMs through our framework reveals that relying on subjective user mediation substantially complicates social reasoning. Furthermore, models are sensitive to user framing, require more detail than humans need to reach correct predictions, and fail to fully leverage clarification questions. We open-source the framework and dataset to encourage future research on user-mediated social reasoning.

AI assistants operate within a user-mediated reality: the assistant hears about social events only through the subjective lens of the user, making it challenging to reason objectively about the true motive of an actor in the user’s circle.

User-mediated reality

When evaluating LLMs’ social reasoning, it’s important to recognize that deployed assistants operate within a user-mediated reality . In classical reasoning tasks like math and code, LLMs operate over objective, complete information. However, when an LLM acts as a conversational assistant and is asked for personal support and advice, it does not observe the actual social interactions firsthand; its only source of

On November 25, 2026, Google Research scientists Zorik Gekhman and Amir Taubenfeld introduced a new evaluation framework and open-source dataset designed to measure how well Large Language Model assistants handle user-mediated social reasoning. The release includes a dataset featuring over 20,000 generated examples built to address the lack of verifiable ground truth in everyday social interactions, where AI assistants must infer hidden motives from subjective, potentially biased user narratives.

The methodology relies on multi-agent simulations built by extending Google's open-source Concordia library. Each simulation features a target entity assigned a controllable hidden motivation interacting with other agents, including a user persona. title: Do We Really Need an LLM for Weight-Space Programming? A Deterministic Forward-Only Paradigm and Its Capability Boundaries
author: Lin Yao
contentSnippet: Recent work on Weight-Space Programming uses LLMs to edit neural weights with forward passes only, conflating LLM scripting with the underlying algebra of forward-only editing. We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.

title: Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
author: Emma Roth
contentSnippet: Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations. Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.” [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lpEWy4Ipy44] As previously reported by Bloomberg, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg. The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

title: Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?
author: Paul Gillin
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 10:59 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026

Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

The popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the o

summary.tldr:
Open-weight artificial intelligence models have rapidly captured enterprise IT market share, shifting strategies away from monolithic reliance on closed frontier APIs toward customizable, cost-effective alternatives. According to Vercel's AI Gateway report, open-weight token traffic surged from 7% in December to 56% in August, with models occupying eight of the top ten spots on OpenRouter's volume rankings. Major market consolidation accompanied this trend, featuring Stripe acquiring OpenRouter for $7.5 billion in August and Nvidia purchasing model hub Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion in September.

Technically, open-weight models span parameters from under 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion, enabling organizations to match specific tasks to smaller engines instead of routing routine workflows through expensive frontier systems. Industry benchmarks and deployments demonstrate significant cost reductions: AT&T shifted 40% of workloads to open models (targeting 70%) and cut AI operating costs by 56% with a mere 2% quality drop; Pinterest achieved over 90% savings; and Uber cut costs per session by over half. High-capacity open models, such as Moonshot AI's 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 and Alibaba's 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max, nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks according to Stanford HAI.

Despite massive cost advantages and enhanced data sovereignty—addressing regulatory demands cited by 79% of AI leaders—experts caution that open weights are not synonymous with traditional open-source software. Commercial licenses vary widely, imposing restrictions based on annual revenue thresholds (such as Liquid AI's $10 million cap), attribution mandates, or acceptable use policies that create potential legal exposure if ignored.
takeaways: **Traffic Surge:** Vercel's AI Gateway reported that open-weight token traffic grew from 7% in December to 56% in August.
**Major M&A Activity:** OpenRouter was acquired by Stripe for $7.5 billion in August, and Nvidia acquired Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion in September.
**Enterprise Cost Reductions:** AT&T cut AI operating costs by 56% by shifting 40% of workloads to open models; Pinterest achieved over 90% cost savings; Uber reduced session costs by over half.
**High-Capacity Performance:** Stanford HAI noted that Moonshot AI's 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 and Alibaba's 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks.

**Licensing Nuances:** Open-weight models do not automatically equal open source; for instance, Liquid AI's models are restricted to commercial use for organizations with under $10 million in annual revenue.

title: AI data centers are becoming harder to build, and neoclouds are feeling it
author: Theresa Loconsolo, Rebecca Bellan
contentSnippet:
⁠Nvidia has made clear⁠ it won’t backstop an AI data center until it’s nearly ready to run, and that’s landing just as neoclouds report construction delays and more expensive debt. The message to developers is that land, power, and a finished building matter more than a pitch deck.

⁠Anita Verma-Lallian⁠ has been selling exactly that. Her company, Arizona Land Consulting, assembles data center sites for developers, hyperscalers, AI labs, and neoclouds, giving her a view into who’s buying, what makes a site viable, and where projects are running into trouble. How community opposition and state-level restrictions are making some markets harder to build in than others.

Utilities getting major customers like TSMC to help fund the infrastructure needed to deliver more power.

Who gets stuck with the bill when a data center project stalls, from developers to lenders to customers.

title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base
author: Nikolay Skachkov
contentSnippet: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.

title: Fuel as Identity: Authenticating Inter-Satellite Laser Links after Total Key Compromise
author: Leon Birkel
contentSnippet: Optical inter-satellite links form the backbone of entire constellations in low Earth orbit, yet their security rests on keys alone. When an attacker obtains every key of a satellite, no secret is left to authenticate it again. Existing fixes fail, since ground rekeying encrypts new keys under the leaked ones, and post-compromise protocols assume an authenticated start. As a remedy, the satellite's orbit can take over as the trust anchor. The attacker then needs an impostor satellite that blocks and retransmits the beam, a chord beneath the curved orbit. Hence, the blocking point lies off free fall and costs the impostor continuous thrust. We formalize this position-gated adversary and prove, for satellites on a shared circular orbit, a tight lower bound on the propellant cost in delta-v of a point-mass craft that keeps blocking, however it moves. We present OrbitLock, a history-chained protocol that combines this position gate with ML-KEM. Each link authenticates on its own, and we sketch how combining links forces an impostor onto every link. Once the chain outlasts an impostor's propellant, every key back to the first is authenticated retroactively. A satellite thus needs no crosslink key before launch, so none can leak in the supply chain. The same mechanism heals the link after total key compromise, even without compromise awareness. A passive attacker is shut out at the next round, whereas an active one splits the chains and is exposed once its propellant runs out. The chain can then heal after an operator reset. As a result, every Starlink satellite has a partner on whose link a CubeSat-class impostor runs out of propellant in about two days. This holds against one rigid craft per link running the best attack we know, if each terminal enforces a 1 km exclusion zone, while the protocol only uses under 0.02% of the link.

title: Same Seed, Different Top Prediction: Cross-Platform Reproducibility of AlphaFold 3 Inference on TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs
author: Lorenzo Pazienza
contentSnippet: AlphaFold 3 returns the highest-ranked of several sampled structures and computes each prediction on one device. Computing centers may schedule them on different GPU types or CPU nodes. Floating-point results can differ between devices, so the same input and seed may return another structure. Neither AlphaFold 3's documentation nor its outputs warn of this. We measure how often the device changes the returned structure, and tell users what to report and how to make devices agree. We used identical inputs, weights, seeds, and settings on two Google tensor processing unit (TPU) generations (v5e, v6e), three NVIDIA GPUs (L4, A100, H100), and an Intel Xeon CPU. On 60 protein-ligand complexes, with five seeds each, switching TPU generations changed the top-ranked sample in 18.0% of 300 predictions. Recompiling never changed it on either TPU, but did so in 7.3% on the L4 GPU. Yet the structures barely moved. The top-ranked pose switched between correct and incorrect in 3.3% to 3.7% of predictions, against about 10% for a new seed. These switches nearly always came from one validity check, with the ligand within 2 angstroms. Follow-ups found the effect again on 72 new targets and between the TPUs and the CPU. Between the A100 and H100 it exceeded recompilation, although AlphaFold 3's developers verified its numerical accuracy on both. An exploratory analysis links the changes to near-tied candidates. We recommend reporting the device and every near-tied sample. A float32 trunk with full-precision matrix products made all five accelerators agree on nearly every prediction.

title: Amazon is reportedly in talks to end Muse AI shopping block
author: Emma Roth
contentSnippet: Amazon has held talks about letting Meta’s Muse AI agent shop on its online marketplace, according to a report from Fortune. The discussions, which could end Amazon’s block on Muse, reportedly center on the kinds of products the AI agent recommends and the potential impact on the ecommerce giant’s advertising revenue. As reported by Fortune, Amazon is concerned that it could lose advertising revenue by allowing Muse on its site, since it depends on actual humans seeing ads across its online marketplace. It’s also reportedly worried about the quality of the product search results that Muse will present to users, as well as whether the AI agent will affect Amazon’s relationship with customers. Neither Amazon nor Meta immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment. Though some online retailers, such as Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, and Sephora, have opened their digital doors to AI agents like Muse, Amazon has been more hesitant. Amazon also blocked Perplexity’s AI agent from shopping on its site, and has instead focused on promoting its own Alexa for Shopping assistant, which customers can now text to shop on their behalf.

title: Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse
author: Lauren Forristal
contentSnippet: Posted: 6:10 AM PST · November 25, 2026 Image Credits: Meta Lauren Forristal Amazon and Meta reportedly in talks to lift blockade on AI agent Muse Amazon may be having a change of heart about Meta’s AI agent, Muse. The two tech giants are reportedly discussing a potential deal that would allow Meta’s popular AI agent to connect directly to Amazon’s store. The talks would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users discovered they were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out. According to a Wednesday report by Fortune , citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about the matter. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement. One of Amazon’s biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business. In October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents. Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace. If Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could ultimately be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers. Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon’s direct relationship with consumers, according to people familiar with the matter. Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies’ CEOs, Fortune also reported. Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch’s requests for comment. title: The questions Jensen Huang and Nvidia will still have to answer about Megaspeed
author: Tim Fernholz
contentSnippet:
Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.

The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.

The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China. Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.

Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers. When it comes to compliance and liability for export-control violations, Nvidia and other chip sellers need assurances that the end users of their chips are obeying the rules. However, they also cannot ignore other information that might call the reliability of those assurances into question, export-control attorneys told TechCrunch.

And that’s why Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was such a problem for Nvidia, likely even more so than her alleged role as a source for Chinese intelligence agencies. If Nvidia personnel, from lower-level employees up to the CEO, had reason to believe that statements from Megaspeed weren’t reliable, the attorneys said, that would increase the company’s legal risk.

“Government investigators likely would want to know, notwithstanding whatever formal assurances were exchanged between the parties, what anyone at Nvidia actually knew about the end use and end users of the chips,” Dan Fisher-Owens, an attorney at the firm Berliner Corcoran & Rowe, told Te

summary.tldr:
Jensen Huang’s return as CEO to Nvidia hasn’t eased the scrutiny the company faces. The chipmaker still needs to address multiple inquiries into allegations that its advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by a customer, the Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed, in violation of U.S. Export rules designed to slow China’s development of frontier AI models.

The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where those chips ended up and whether Huang’s affair with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed’s assurances. Huang’s return doesn’t settle that. Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested Nvidia isn’t a target of an investigation, but California’s attorney general and Congress are pressing ahead, and the Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating, too.
takeaways: Government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that some of the chips Megaspeed bought for data center projects in Malaysia were in fact being diverted to China.
Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
Diversion of this kind would be a fairly routine issue for a company like Nvidia, whose in-demand chips are the targets of smugglers and resellers.

title: Can Large Language Models Estimate the Likely Technological Impact of Scientific Research? Evidence from Biotechnology
author: Zhiyu Tao
contentSnippet: This study provides large-scale empirical evidence about whether large language model (LLM)-based assessments of the likely technological impact of scientific publications are associated with their patent-based impact. Using Lens.org, we constructed a biotechnology dataset of 107,615 papers published between 1980 and 2015 with their patent citation counts. We used GPT-5-mini, Qwen-Flash, and DeepSeek-V3.2 to estimate papers technological impact and technology relevance, benchmarking model outputs against log-transformed patent-citation counts through correlation analysis, distributional alignment, and lift-over-random measures. The results show that LLMs extract meaningful signals associated with technological impact from scientific text, although there are substantial differences at the meso-level such as between research fields, journals, and countries. LLMs also outperform random selection in screening for papers with high observed patent impact. Overall, this study identifies the strengths, contexts, and limitations of LLM-based technological impact evaluation and highlights its potential to support large-scale screening for scientific work with downstream technological value.

title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
author: Alessio Devoto
contentSnippet: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.

title: Characterization and empirical correction of a spatially coherent spectral artifact in Gemini/GMOS-N IFU observations
author: Xiaoyang Chen
contentSnippet: We report a recurring spectral artifact identified in observations obtained with the integral field unit (IFU) of the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on the Gemini North telescope (GMOS-N). The artifact appears as a vertically aligned structure in reconstructed images of the IFU field of view, associated with a specific group of fibers and exhibiting a broad spectral feature around 8000~\AAng. Similar features were repeatedly identified in observations of different astronomical targets obtained between 2020 and 2022 using the R150 grating in the two-slit IFU mode. Taking advantage of the reproducibility of the artifact in the fiber and wavelength domains, we develop an empirical correction method in which the artifact is modeled as the product of a common spectral profile and a fiber-dependent amplitude distribution, with an overall normalization determined independently for each exposure. The artifact template is constructed from observations in which the affected fibers are largely separated from the astronomical source and subsequently applied to independent observations in which the artifact overlaps the source. The correction substantially suppresses the artificial spatial structure in the reconstructed images. Although the physical origin of the artifact remains unidentified, we present its observational characteristics and correction procedure to facilitate the identification and treatment of similar features by other GMOS-IFU users.

title: Improving Tail-Augmented Speculative Drafting with Hidden State Mixing and Gradient Detach
author: Yaniv Galron
contentSnippet: Multi-token prediction (MTP) modules and EAGLE-style drafters support efficient speculative decoding by reusing target-model hidden states. Their autoregressive use, however, introduces a training-inference mismatch: training supplies sequences of hidden states from the backbone or a single MTP step, whereas inference attends to a target-model prefix followed by a growing tail of recurrently generated MTP states. EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) explicitly simulates this behavior during training, at the cost of additional memory and specialized attention masks. We introduce two training-only methods for improving autoregressive drafting. Hidden State Mixing (HSM) samples among backbone and MTP hidden states aligned to the same prediction target, exposing the drafter to mixtures of states from different MTP steps without explicitly simulating inference. Hidden State Gradient Detach (HSGD) is a regularization method that stochastically blocks gradients through hidden state and embedding pathways while preserving the forward computation. Neither method adds inference cost. In joint pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning, HSGD yields the highest acceptance rates at early draft positions, while HSM performs best later in the draft. These acceptance rate trends favor HSM for long-draft-length serving and HSGD for short-draft-length serving. Furthermore, across four Nemotron models and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, HSM-based MTP boosting with a frozen backbone improves mean acceptance length by up to 52.2% over the co-trained MTP. For EAGLE-3 drafters, HSM offers competitive acceptance with TTT, with 48% lower peak reserved training memory in a four-step Qwen3-8B comparison. HSM implementations are publicly available in Megatron-LM and NVIDIA Model Optimizer.

title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
author: Matthew King
contentSnippet: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy. Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”  Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.  As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.  Transparency, monetized The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by st

title: A Nationwide Snapshot of Starlink Affordability
author: Shaddi Hasan
contentSnippet: Starlink positions itself as "fast affordable Internet" that can provide service to nearly every household in the United States, and is slated to be responsible for providing the only broadband service to a significant number of US households via the NTIA's BEAD program. However, neither the FCC's National Broadband Map nor Starlink's own availability map captures what service costs. We present the first national census of Starlink's residential broadband pricing. We first identify that Starlink's offers are uniform within H3 resolution 6 grid cells, allowing us to collect plans and prices for every populated cell in the United States, more than 162,000 addresses, in October 2026. We find that while Starlink's service prices are fairly consistent, the effective price of the most affordable plan varies across the country, driven by restricting sales of less expensive plans as well as "demand surcharges" ranging between \$100 and \$1,500. Using a common affordability threshold of 2% of monthly income, we find that service restrictions or surcharges make Starlink unaffordable for approximately 4.3 million households, and in total nearly a quarter of all US households (roughly 25.5 million) cannot afford Starlink. Finally, approximately 80% of locations where Starlink is slated to receive BEAD funding face no constrained pricing today.

title: On Grokking and the Dynamics of Generalization
author: Malik Amir
contentSnippet: We extend the signal-channel theory of grokking introduced by Litman and Guo by relating training dissipation and evaluation transfer to population risk. For preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels, we distinguish two sources of limited evaluation visibility, namely small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer. We obtain quantitative bounds for task visibility and establish their stability under signal filtering and changes of evaluation distribution. We describe how task directions enter the effective signal channel through spectral activation or transport. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the transferred signal to decrease squared population risk and derive classification error bounds under margin assumptions. These results yield sufficient conditions for the same training trajectory to generalize under one evaluation distribution while failing under another. We show that differences in spectral learning rates can produce arbitrarily long delays between low training loss and low population risk. By relating classification accuracy to the distribution of margin crossing times, we construct a family of gradient flows in which the generalization delay tends to infinity, while both the duration of the transition from zero to full accuracy and the corresponding variation of population risk tend to zero. These phenomena occur without feature evolution during training. Finally, we prove that the occurrence and timing of generalization cannot generally be inferred from training dynamics alone, but depend on the geometry of evaluation transfer and its relation to the target.
